q: On what basis does the Turing Test judge whether a machine is intelligent?
options: Whether a human judge can no longer tell it apart from a person
Whether it reasons internally in the same way a human brain does
Whether it can process information faster than a human can
Whether it was built using biologically inspired methods
explain: A machine passes when a judge cannot tell its replies from a person's. The test looks only at behaviour, so how the machine works, its speed or brain-like design does not matter.

q: A human judge talks to a hidden entity and cannot tell whether it is a computer. What does the Turing Test conclude about the computer?
options: The computer has shown that it is conscious and self-aware
The computer has passed the test and is said to be intelligent
The judge has failed and the test must be repeated with a new judge
The computer has become a form of strong AI by definition
explain: Passing is defined by the judge being unable to tell the difference. This says nothing about consciousness, so it does not make the machine strong AI.

q: Which question did Turing put in place of asking whether machines can think?
options: Can machines store more knowledge than any human?
Can machines describe their own thoughts accurately?
Can machines pass a behaviour test for intelligence?
Can machines copy the structure of a human brain?
explain: Thinking is hard to define and measure, so Turing replaced it with a question about behaviour that can be tested. The other options ask about stored knowledge, self-reports or brain structure.

q: Which statements about the two words in the term artificial intelligence are correct?
options: Intelligence has one agreed test that gives a single score
Artificial means produced by human effort rather than arising naturally
Both words are equally disputed and have no agreed meaning
Intelligence is hard to define because it is hard to measure
explain: People broadly agree what artificial means, but intelligence is hard to define. It has no single agreed measure.

q: A voice assistant answers set questions using predefined instructions and parameters. How is it best classified?
options: Strong AI, because it understands speech and language as well as a human does
Strong AI, because it can plan for the future in its own way
Weak AI, because it lacks the memory needed for any learning
Weak AI, because it solves one limited task, not the full human range
explain: Assistants such as Siri and Alexa are narrow systems built for specific problems. The option about lacking memory fails because weak AI can still learn from data.

q: Which statements describe strong AI?
options: It aims to be indistinguishable from the human mind
It is already in everyday use in chatbots and phones
It is designed to solve one specific problem only
It would be able to plan for the future and be creative
It would have self-awareness and consciousness
explain: Strong AI is a theoretical goal, a machine with human-level intelligence. Systems in everyday use are narrow weak AI.

q: Which statements about weak AI are correct?
options: It has consciousness but only a narrow range of tasks
Most or all of today's AI systems are examples of it
It exists only as a theoretical concept
It does not cover the full range of human cognitive abilities
It generates output from predefined instructions and parameters
It is built to solve a specific problem
explain: Weak AI is the practical form that exists now. Consciousness and a purely theoretical status describe strong AI instead.

q: A chess program always returns the same move for the same board and keeps no memory of earlier games. Which type of AI is this?
options: A reactive machine
A limited memory machine
A theory of mind system
A self-aware system
explain: Reactive machines have no memory and are task specific, so an input always gives the same output. Deep Blue is the standard example.

q: Which statements describe limited memory machines?
options: Deep learning systems such as ChatGPT are examples
They can look at the past and monitor objects over time
They get better as they receive more data to train on
They always give the same output for the same input with no memory
They have a conscious understanding of their own existence
explain: Limited memory machines look at the past and improve with more data. Giving the same output with no memory describes reactive machines, and a conscious understanding of existence describes self-aware systems.

q: Which ability marks theory of mind AI, as opposed to systems that only match patterns?
options: Reproducing identical outputs every time from a fixed set of statistical rules
Understanding human motives and intentions and predicting behaviour
Monitoring one object over time without understanding it
Having a conscious sense of its own existence
explain: Theory of mind AI would understand human motives and intentions, not just match patterns. Monitoring one object over time describes limited memory machines, and a conscious sense of existence describes self-aware AI, which is a later step.

q: Which type of AI does not exist yet, partly because too little is known about the human brain and emotion?
options: Reactive machines
Limited memory machines
Self-aware machines
Deep learning systems
explain: Self-aware AI would understand itself as well as the world around it. Reactive machines, limited memory machines and deep learning systems already exist.

q: Which of these are among the four types of AI, ordered from simple to advanced?
options: Self-awareness
Weak AI
Limited memory machines
Reactive machines
Theory of mind
Strong AI
explain: Weak and strong AI are a separate split, based on how broad the ability is. The four types are ordered by memory and understanding.

q: What does the theory of multiple intelligences claim?
options: Intelligence is one general ability that can be measured by one score
Only logical and mathematical skill counts as true intelligence
Each kind of intelligence is found only in humans, never in machines
Intelligence is made of several distinct kinds, not one general ability
explain: The theory separates intelligence into several kinds. So whether a machine is intelligent depends on which kind is meant.

q: Which intelligence is the ability to perceive, understand and manage emotions, with sensitivity to other people's moods?
options: Interpersonal intelligence
Intrapersonal intelligence
Naturalistic intelligence
Existential intelligence
explain: Interpersonal intelligence is sensitivity to the moods and motives of others and the ability to work in groups. Intrapersonal intelligence is about self-reflection.

q: Someone has a deep understanding of themselves and is good at introspection. Which intelligence is this?
options: Interpersonal intelligence
Intrapersonal intelligence
Bodily-kinesthetic intelligence
Linguistic-verbal intelligence
explain: Intrapersonal intelligence looks inward at the self. The tempting wrong choice is interpersonal intelligence, which looks outward at other people.

q: A rover identifies and classifies rocks and features of its environment. Which human intelligence does this resemble most?
options: Existential intelligence
Linguistic-verbal intelligence
Naturalistic intelligence
Visual-spatial intelligence
explain: Naturalistic intelligence is the ability to identify, classify and manipulate elements of the environment. Visual-spatial is about spatial judgement and visualisation.

q: Which pairs correctly match an intelligence with its description?
options: Logical-mathematical with logic, abstraction and reasoning about causal systems
Visual-spatial with a talent for numbers and critical thinking
Bodily-kinesthetic with control of body movement and skilful handling of objects
Existential with the ability to identify animals and plants
Linguistic-verbal with a facility for words, reading and writing
explain: Visual-spatial intelligence is about spatial problems, and numbers and critical thinking belong to logical-mathematical intelligence. Existential intelligence is about the meaning of life, and identifying animals and plants belongs to naturalistic intelligence.

q: A system reaches intelligent behaviour by a method that looks nothing like human thought. From the behavioural view of AI, is this a problem?
options: Yes, because only biologically observable methods count as AI
Yes, because the method must match how humans reason
No, but only if the system also has consciousness
No, because the outcome matters and the method does not
explain: In a computing context what matters is the behaviour produced. The definition of AI does not have to be confined to biologically observable methods.

q: Explain what the Turing Test is and how a computer passes it.
model: The Turing Test is a way of defining AI by behaviour instead of asking whether a machine can really think. A human judge communicates with a hidden entity and has to decide whether it is a computer or a person. If the judge cannot tell, the computer passes and is said to be intelligent. The test cares about the outcome, so it ignores how the machine produces its answers. It replaced the hard question of whether machines think with a question that can be tested.
points: It tests whether a machine can show intelligent behaviour equal to a human
A human judge cannot tell if the other entity is a computer
If the judge fails to tell, the computer has passed and counts as intelligent
It focuses on behaviour and not on intellect or how the machine works

q: Compare weak AI and strong AI and give one example of weak AI.
model: Weak AI is built to solve a specific problem using predefined instructions and parameters. It does not cover the full range of human cognitive ability. Almost all of today's AI is weak, for example Siri, Alexa or a self driving car. Strong AI would match human intelligence, with self awareness, consciousness, creativity and the ability to plan for the future. It exists only as a theoretical idea with today's technology, so no real system is an example.
points: Weak AI solves limited specific problems
Strong AI would equal human intelligence and have self awareness
Gives one correct example of weak AI, such as a voice assistant or chatbot
Strong AI only exists as a theoretical concept today

q: Compare reactive machines with limited memory machines.
model: A reactive machine has no memory and is built for one task, so the same input always gives the same output. It relies on statistics, fixed rules and pattern recognition, and a chess program or a recommendation system is an example. A limited memory machine can look at the past and track objects or situations over time. It copies how neurons in the brain work together, so it gets better as it trains on more data. Deep learning systems such as ChatGPT are examples.
points: Reactive machines have no memory and give the same output for the same input
Limited memory machines can look into the past and monitor things over time
Limited memory machines improve with more training data
One correct example of each, such as Deep Blue and ChatGPT

q: Describe the four types of AI and say which one does not exist yet.
model: The four types run from simple to advanced. Reactive machines have no memory and give fixed outputs. Limited memory machines learn from data and look at the past. Theory of mind AI would understand human motives and intentions and predict behaviour, and it would be broad rather than limited to one domain. Self aware AI would have a conscious sense of its own existence. Self awareness does not exist yet because we do not know enough about the human brain and emotion.
points: Names all four types in order
Reactive machines have no memory and limited memory machines learn from past data
Theory of mind understands motives and intentions
Self awareness is a sense of self and does not exist yet

q: Explain why artificial intelligence is hard to define even though the word artificial is easy to agree on.
model: Artificial means produced by human effort rather than arising naturally, and people broadly agree on that. Intelligence is a different matter because it means intellect, wisdom and understanding, which are very hard to measure. Without a clear measure it is hard to say when a machine has it. The theory of multiple intelligences adds to the problem because it splits intelligence into several kinds. This is why the Turing Test uses behaviour as a practical definition.
points: Artificial has basic agreement on its meaning
Intelligence is hard to define because it is hard to measure
Intelligence may have several modalities and not one single form
Behaviour based tests offer a practical way around the problem

q: Explain the theory of multiple intelligences and describe two of the types.
model: The theory says that human intelligence is not one general ability but is split into specific modalities. Visual-spatial intelligence is spatial judgement and the ability to picture objects from different angles, for example when navigating. Linguistic-verbal intelligence is a skill with words and languages, such as reading, writing and telling stories. Other types include logical-mathematical, bodily-kinesthetic, naturalistic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and existential. Each type raises the question of whether a machine could have it.
points: Intelligence is split into modalities and not one general ability
Describes one type correctly
Describes a second type correctly
Names at least one other type, or says each type raises the question of whether a machine could have it

q: Explain why the computing definition of AI focuses on behaviour and not on how the machine works.
model: Asking whether a machine truly thinks cannot be answered because intelligence is hard to define and measure. The computing definition therefore says AI is the ability of a machine to mimic the behaviour of living things, mainly humans. How the machine does this is not important and what matters is the outcome. This follows from the Turing Test, which only asks whether a judge can tell the machine apart from a person. The definition also does not require the machine to copy biological methods.
points: Thinking and intelligence are hard to define or measure
AI means a machine mimicking behaviour of living entities
The method does not matter and the outcome does
Links the focus on behaviour to the Turing Test

q: Describe theory of mind AI and explain how it differs from classic pattern matching systems.
model: Theory of mind AI would be able to understand human motives, intentions and reasoning and predict behaviour, as if simulating human relationships. It could place information in context. It would have broad functionality, whereas classic machine learning algorithms only work well in one specific domain. The key difference is that it would not just match patterns but would understand them. This type is often linked to artificial general intelligence.
points: Understands human motives and intentions and predicts behaviour
Can contextualise information
Broad functionality compared with narrow domain algorithms
Understands patterns and does not only match them
